weeks.title: Expressions and equations
weeks.big_idea: Expressions name quantities. Equivalent forms describe the same quantity. Equations can be solved by keeping both sides equal.
weeks.connections: Ratios and fraction division help solve equations. These same equations will describe proportional relationships.
weeks.omissions: Core one-step equations only. Multi-step rational equations, formal inequalities with several steps, and a full survey of algebraic properties are deferred.

weeks.title: Area and surface area
weeks.big_idea: Area counts square units that cover a surface. Cutting and rearranging reveal triangle and parallelogram formulas. A net helps count every face of a solid.
weeks.connections: Multiplication and fraction multiplication measure flat regions. Nets connect those regions to three-dimensional solids.
weeks.omissions: Surface area is limited to rectangular prisms, right triangular prisms, and square pyramids. Non-square pyramid bases, cylinders, and complex composite solids are deferred.

weeks.title: Negative numbers, coordinates, and inequalities
weeks.big_idea: A signed number gives a position relative to zero. Coordinates use two such positions. Inequalities describe all positions that meet a condition.
weeks.connections: Number lines extend fraction and decimal ideas to negatives. Coordinates will show proportional relationships and data.
weeks.omissions: Signed-number operations remain previews. GCF and LCM receive short weekday instruction and basic practice, without elaborate word problems or prime-factor methods.

sessions.title: Scale and proportional relationships
sessions.goal: Use scale factors and identify relationships with a constant rate per one.
sessions.key_idea: A scaled copy multiplies every length by the same factor. Proportional relationships have the form y = kx.
sessions.prerequisite: Ratios, unit rates, rectangle area, and coordinate graphs.

vocab.meaning: The multiplier from an original length to a copy length.
vocab.example: A factor of 2 doubles every length.

vocab.meaning: A shape with matching angles and one multiplier for every length.
The same y per one x in a proportional relationship.
Related by a fixed multiplier with zero matched to zero.

problems.text: A 4 cm by 6 cm rectangle is copied with scale factor 2. Find the new side lengths and compare areas.
problems.answer: 8 cm by 12 cm; area 24 to 96 square cm, factor 4
problems.case: whole-number scale factor; area factor squared
problems.worked: Both dimensions double, so four originals fit in the copy.
problems.error: Applies the length factor once to area.

problems.text: A triangle has side lengths 6, 8, and 10 cm. Copy it with scale factor {1/2}. Find its side lengths. What happens to its angles?
problems.case: fractional scale factor; unchanged angles
problems.worked: Multiply every length by one half. Matching sides have the same ratio.
problems.error: Subtracts one from each length instead of multiplying.

problems.text: A map uses 1 cm for 25 km. Two towns are 3.6 cm apart on the map. Find their actual distance.
problems.case: map scale with units; decimal length
problems.worked: Each map centimeter represents 25 km, so multiply 3.6 × 25.
problems.error: Reverses map and actual units.

problems.text: A drawing has area 5 square cm. A scaled copy has all lengths three times as large. Find its area.
problems.case: area multiplier is square of length multiplier
problems.worked: There are three times as many units in each of two directions: factor 9.
problems.error: Uses the length factor for area.

problems.text: A table pairs x = 1, 2, 4 with y = 2.5, 5, 10. Find k and write y = kx.
problems.case: proportional table; unit rate; equation
problems.worked: Each y divided by its x gives 2.5.
problems.error: Finds x per y instead of y per x.

problems.text: Compare two straight-line graphs: A passes through (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4). B passes through (0, 3), (1, 5), (2, 7). Which is proportional?
problems.answer: A: y = 2x. B is not proportional because it starts at 3 when x = 0.
problems.case: graph through origin versus nonzero intercept
problems.worked: Both have equal increases, but only A has zero output for zero input.
problems.error: Mistakes constant differences for a constant ratio.

diagram.caption: Graph A starts at zero. Graph B starts at 3.

problems.text: A ride costs $4 to start and $3 per mile. Write cost c for m miles. Is it proportional?
problems.case: non-proportional story with fixed fee
problems.worked: At zero miles the cost is $4. Cost per mile changes as the fee is spread out.
problems.error: Treats the starting fee as a per-mile charge.

problems.text: A faucet fills {3/4} liter in {1/2} minute at a constant rate. Write liters L after t minutes.
problems.case: fractional unit rate; equation from a story
problems.worked: Double the half-minute amount to get 1.5 liters per minute.
problems.error: Reverses liters per minute and minutes per liter.

exit.text: A table pairs x = 1, 3, 5 with y = 5, 11, 17. Is y proportional to x? Support your answer with ratios or the value at zero.
exit.answer: No. Ratios 5, {11/3}, {17/5} differ. The rule y = 3x + 2 gives y = 2 at zero.
exit.case: constant difference does not prove proportionality
exit.worked: The change in y is always 6 when x increases by 2, but the ratio y to x is not constant.
exit.wrong: Yes, y increases by 6 each time
exit.error: Uses additive pattern instead of a constant multiplier.

error.text: Eli triples every length of a drawing. He says its area also triples. Explain and repair his claim.
error.correction: The area is multiplied by 9 because both dimensions are tripled.
error.why: Applies one length multiplier to a two-dimensional measure.
error.move: Tile a 3 by 3 array of original rectangles.

example.text: A copy of a 3 cm by 5 cm rectangle uses scale factor 2.
steps: The new lengths are 6 cm and 10 cm.
The original area is 15 square cm; the copy area is 60 square cm.
The area factor is 60 ÷ 15 = 4 = 2².

misconceptions.why: Confuses additive change with scaling.
misconceptions.move: Compare each copy-to-original ratio.

sessions.title: Circles and first previews
sessions.goal: Find circle measures and connect percent change and signed steps to earlier models.
sessions.key_idea: Circumference measures the boundary. Circle area uses the square of the radius. π is exact; 3.14 is an approximation.
sessions.prerequisite: Area, squares, percent of a whole, and negative-number order.

vocab.meaning: Distance from the center to the circle.
vocab.example: A radius of 3 cm gives diameter 6 cm.

vocab.meaning: Distance across the circle through its center.
The distance around a circle.
The ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

problems.text: A circle has diameter 8 cm. Find its circumference in terms of π and using 3.14.
problems.case: circumference from diameter; exact and approximate
problems.worked: C = πd = 8π. Approximate with 8 × 3.14.
problems.error: Uses a squared length for a boundary.

diagram.caption: The diameter goes through the center.

problems.text: A circle has radius 3 cm. Find its diameter and circumference in terms of π.
problems.case: circumference from radius
problems.worked: Double the radius before multiplying by π.
problems.error: Uses the radius as the diameter.

problems.text: Find the area of a circle with radius 4 cm. Give an exact answer and an approximation using 3.14.
problems.case: area from radius; exact and approximate
problems.worked: A = πr². Square the radius first, then multiply by π.
problems.error: Uses circumference as area.

problems.text: A circle has diameter 6 cm. Find its area in terms of π and using 3.14.
problems.case: area from diameter; halve first
problems.worked: The radius is 3 cm, so A = π × 3² = 9π.
problems.error: Squares the diameter.

problems.text: Circle A has diameter 4 cm and circumference 4π cm. Circle B has diameter 10 cm and circumference 10π cm. Compare C ÷ d.
problems.case: constant circumference-to-diameter ratio
problems.worked: Each circumference is π times its diameter. Dividing by the diameter leaves π.
problems.wrong: The larger circle has the larger ratio
problems.error: Confuses a larger circumference with a larger ratio.

problems.text: A collection grows from 80 cards to 100. Find the percent increase. Then find the percent decrease from 100 back to 80.
problems.case: percent increase and decrease; original whole
problems.worked: The same change of 20 is compared with different starting amounts.
problems.error: Uses the first starting value for both changes.

problems.text: Start with 80 tokens. Increase by 25%, then decrease the result by 25%. Find the final amount. Explain why it is not 80.
problems.answer: 75 tokens; the decrease uses the larger whole 100
problems.case: equal percent increase and decrease do not cancel
problems.worked: First add 20. Then subtract 25 from 100. The percent applies to a new starting amount.
problems.error: Assumes equal percentages are equal amounts.

problems.text: Use steps on a number line for −2 + 5, −3 + (−4), and 2 − 6.
problems.case: positive addend; negative addend; subtraction across zero
problems.worked: A positive addend moves right. A negative addend or subtracting a positive moves left.
problems.error: Adds distances without direction.

diagram.caption: Adding 5 moves five units to the right.

exit.text: A circle has diameter 12 cm. Find its area in terms of π and using 3.14. Show the radius you used.
exit.answer: Radius 6 cm; area 36π square cm; about 113.04 square cm
exit.error: Squares the diameter instead of the radius.

diagram.caption: Find the radius before the area.

error.text: Maya finds area from a diameter of 14 cm by writing π × 14² = 196π. Explain and repair it.
error.correction: Radius = 7 cm, so area = 49π square cm.
error.why: Uses diameter where the formula requires radius.
error.move: Mark the center and split the diameter into two equal radii.

example.text: Find area when a circle’s diameter is 10 m.
steps: The radius is half the diameter: 5 m.
Square the radius: 5² = 25.
Area = 25π square m, or about 78.5 square m using 3.14.

fade.text: A circle has diameter 16 cm. Complete: radius = __; area = π × __² = __π square cm.

look_fors.response: Marks the center and halves the diameter.
look_fors.move: Ask which segment runs from center to circle.

look_fors.response: Names linear versus square units.
look_fors.move: Trace the edge, then shade the interior.

look_fors.response: Uses a percent table or a tape to track the new whole.
look_fors.why: Both models can show why changes do not cancel.
look_fors.move: Accept either and label the starting amount for each step.

misconceptions.response: Squares the diameter.
misconceptions.why: Uses the given number without identifying it.
misconceptions.move: Mark two equal radii along the diameter.

misconceptions.response: Writes π = 3.14 exactly.
misconceptions.why: Confuses approximation with an exact constant.
misconceptions.move: Keep the π form and label the decimal answer about.

misconceptions.response: Cancels equal percent increases and decreases.
misconceptions.why: Ignores the changed whole.
misconceptions.move: Write the starting amount beside each percent calculation.

discussion: Partner compare: How can the units tell us which circle formula fits?
Agree or disagree: A 25% increase and a 25% decrease return to the start. Use 80 tokens.
